analysis.one_liner: Cuts the capital gains tax rates investors pay on profits from selling assets.
analysis.headline: The bill to cut the top capital gains tax rate from 20% to 15% was referred to the Senate Finance Committee on June 24, 1998 and never advanced further before the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would cut the top federal tax rate on capital gains — profits from selling stocks, businesses, real estate, and other assets — from 20% to 15%, and cut the rate paid by taxpayers in lower brackets from 10% to 7.5%. It would also shorten from 18 months to one year the time an investor must hold an asset to qualify for the lower rate, and apply the new rates within the alternative minimum tax as well. The tax cut would take effect for gains on or after June 24, 1998, including part-way through that tax year.
analysis.who_benefits: Investors who sell stocks, bonds, businesses, and other appreciated assets — the households that own most capital gains. Capital gains income is heavily concentrated at the top: most households realize little or no capital gain in a given year, while the largest gains are reported by high-income taxpayers. A cut from 20% to 15% on the top rate, plus a shorter one-year holding requirement that makes it easier to qualify sooner, would deliver the largest dollar savings to those with the biggest gains. Anyone selling a home or business at a profit would pay somewhat less tax, but the benefits scale with the size of the gain.
analysis.who_benefits_short: High-income investors with large asset gains

how_it_helps.text: Cuts the top capital gains rate from 20% to 15%, reducing the tax owed when investors sell stocks, businesses, and other assets held over one year [S3].
Cuts the capital gains rate for taxpayers in lower income-tax brackets from 10% to 7.5%, so smaller gains are taxed less as well [S3].
Shortens the qualifying holding period from 18 months to 1 year, letting investors get the lower rate a year sooner [S3].
Applies the new lower rates under the alternative minimum tax and to foreign-investor withholding, so the cut reaches taxpayers who would otherwise be taxed at the higher AMT rate [S3].

analysis.who_pays: The federal Treasury: lower capital gains rates mean less revenue, which would either be made up through other taxes, more borrowing, or smaller public spending. In practice, since capital gains are concentrated among the wealthiest households, the tax saving flows to them while the cost of replacing the lost revenue falls on everyone else or on future taxpayers through debt. There is no offsetting revenue provision in the bill.
analysis.who_pays_short: Federal taxpayers and the Treasury overall

drawbacks.text: The benefits go almost entirely to households with the largest asset gains — mostly high-income investors — because most ordinary families realize little or no taxable capital gain in a year [S3].
The bill contains no way to pay for the lost revenue, so the cut would add to deficits or force other taxes or spending to fill the gap [S3].
Cutting the rate for gains held one year or more reduces the tax penalty for quickly flipping assets, which could push investors toward shorter-term trading rather than long-term holding [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For the investors with large gains, the benefit is straightforward: a lower rate on every dollar of profit from selling assets. For everyone else, the value is indirect — the argument supporters would make is that lower capital gains taxes encourage investment and economic growth, but the bill itself guarantees that its direct tax savings are concentrated among households that own the most assets, and it funds none of the revenue loss. The bill's own text confirms the distribution: it cuts the top rate on the largest gains while also trimming the 10% rate to 7.5% for smaller gains, which softens but does not change where the money goes.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced on June 24, 1998, sent to the Senate Finance Committee, and the Congress ended on January 3, 1999 without the committee or the full Senate ever acting on it.

narrative.text: Senate Majority Leader Trent Lott and 34 Republican senators introduced the bill on June 24, 1998 [S1].
The same day it was read twice and referred to the Senate Finance Committee, which held it; no markup, committee vote, or floor action followed [S5].
The 105th Congress ended on January 3, 1999, and the bill died in committee with no vote ever taken [S1].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Capital gains tax rates stayed at the levels set by the 1997 Taxpayer Relief Act rather than dropping to the proposed 15% top rate, so the federal Treasury kept the revenue. No one won the cut the bill promised, but taxpayers generally avoided the lost revenue it would have caused.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: The Treasury; investors got no cut

against.what_they_did: Never took up the bill after referral; it sat in committee until the Congress ended

sides.party_line_note: All 34 cosponsors, plus the sponsor, were Republicans; no Democrat signed on, and the bill never reached a floor vote.

industries.note: These are the households that report most capital gains and would have received most of the tax savings from the 20%-to-15% cut. The bill's death left their tax rate unchanged.
Because the bill never became law, the federal government kept the revenue that a capital gains rate cut would have removed, avoiding pressure for offsetting tax increases or borrowing.

Brokers, fund managers, and the investment industry generally benefit from lower capital gains rates, which make selling appreciated assets cheaper for their clients and can increase trading and asset sales. The bill would have shortened the holding period to one year, increasing trading activity, but it never advanced.
